issues.body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/647
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

> **Stacked on #1495** (the persistent/ephemeral split + scope-based read/write API). Review/merge that first; this diff is against that branch. Carries the same latest-`main` merge as #1495.

## What

The final step of the #1433 reorder: extract the **persistent-checkpoint contract** into a new `github.com/entireio/cli/api/checkpoint` package — born with the persistent vocabulary and scope-based names (the whole reason we did the rename before relocating).

**Moved to `api/checkpoint`:**
- Persisted document types: `Metadata`, `CheckpointSummary`, `Summary`/`LearningsSummary`/`CodeLearning`, `Attribution`, `SessionFilePaths`, `SessionMetrics`, `CheckpointInfo`, `SessionContent`.
- Option types: `WriteOptions`, `UpdateOptions`, `PrecomputedTranscriptBlobs`.
- Contract surface:
  - read tiers `CheckpointReader` (`Read`, `List`) + `SessionReader` (the four session reads), composed into `PersistentStore`;
  - `Writer` + the sealed `WriteRequest` union (`Session` / `SessionTranscript` / `SessionSummary` / `CheckpointAttribution`);
  - the reader helpers (`ReadCheckpoint`, `ReadLatestSessionContent`, `ReadRawSessionLogForCheckpoint`), the sentinel errors, and `CheckpointVersionBranchV1`.

The contract depends only on **leaf** packages (`agent/types`, `checkpoint/id`, `redact`, go-git `plumbing`) — a backend can implement it without the CLI's agent/TUI/git machinery.

**Stays in `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint`:** `GitStore` + methods, `Open`, the `Stores` facade, `PersistentRefs`, `AuthorReader`, `normalizeCheckpointSummary`, and the entire git-only ephemeral surface.

## Zero call-site churn

`cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint` imports the contract and re-exports every moved symbol via aliases (`aliases.go`):

```go
type CheckpointSummary = apicheckpoint.CheckpointSummary
var  ErrCheckpointNotFound = apicheckpoint.ErrCheckpointNotFound
func ReadCheckpoint(...) (...) { return apicheckpoint.ReadCheckpoint(...) }
```

All existing importers compile unchanged; the backend imports `api/checkpoint` directly. (Helpers are thin wrapper funcs, not mutable vars — addressing the earlier review note.)

## Cleanup (post-review `/simplify` pass)
- Extracted a shared `getSessionTree` helper: the four `SessionReader` methods each repeated the same context-check → fetching-tree → checkpoint-tree → session-subtree navigation (with identical `ErrCheckpointNotFound` wrapping) before reading their files. Behavior unchanged.

## Notes
- `PrecomputedTranscriptBlobs.isUsable` → exported `IsUsable` (its one caller is now across the package boundary).
- The `Write` union is sealed to `api/checkpoint`, so the impl-package unknown-request test was dropped (no longer expressible); per-request dispatch coverage remains.
- Doc-comment terminology aligned to "persistent" (was "committed") on the moved option types.

## Verification
`go build ./...`, full `go test ./...`, and `mise run lint` (0 issues) green; validated with `codex exec review` (which confirmed `errors.Is` still works across the alias boundary) and a 4-agent `/simplify` review (reuse / simplification / efficiency / altitude).

issues.title: Fix multi-session attribution summary loss
issues.body:
Fix multi-session attribution summary loss                                                              
                                                                                                          
  When multiple agent sessions contribute to the same checkpoint (same base commit), per-session          
  InitialAttribution data was being lost during condensation — the root CheckpointSummary only reflected  
  the latest session's attribution, not the aggregate across all sessions.                                
                                                                                                          
  This PR fixes the problem with three changes:

  1. Combined attribution on CheckpointSummary                                                            
   
  - Adds a combined_attribution field to CheckpointSummary that holds the summed attribution across all   
  sessions in a checkpoint                                                                              
  - After all sessions are condensed in PostCommit, updateCombinedAttributionForCheckpoint reads each     
  session's InitialAttribution, aggregates the line counts (agent lines, human added/modified/removed,    
  total committed), and writes the result back to the root metadata
  - Existing combined_attribution is preserved when the summary is rewritten by subsequent session        
  condensations                                                                                           
   
  2. Lightweight ReadSessionMetadata path                                                                 
                                                                                                        
  - Adds GitStore.ReadSessionMetadata() that reads only metadata.json for a given session index — no      
  transcript or prompt blobs                                                                            
  - Used by the aggregation logic to avoid expensive full-content reads when only attribution data is     
  needed                                                                                                  
   
  3. Diagnostic prompt_attributions persistence                                                           
                                                                                                        
  - Persists raw per-prompt attribution diagnostics (PromptAttributions) as JSON in each session's        
  metadata.json
  - Wired through both v1 and v2 committed checkpoint writers                                             
  - Enables root-cause analysis of attribution bugs by showing exactly which prompt recorded which "user" 
  lines

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Updates checkpoint metadata schema and post-commit behavior to persist new diagnostic attribution data and to mutate root checkpoint metadata after writes; errors could affect checkpoint history or attribution reporting for existing multi-session checkpoints.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes multi-session attribution loss by introducing a root-level `combined_attribution` field on `CheckpointSummary` and updating it after all sessions are condensed.
> 
> Adds a cheap `ReadSessionMetadata` path plus `UpdateCheckpointSummary` to recompute/sum per-session `initial_attribution` and persist the aggregate without rewriting session content; root summary writes now preserve any existing `combined_attribution` instead of dropping it.
> 
> Also persists raw per-prompt attribution diagnostics by JSON-encoding `PromptAttributions` into session `metadata.json` (`prompt_attributions`), and wires this through both v1 and v2 committed checkpoint writers. Includes a regression test covering multi-session combined attribution persistence.
> 
> <sup>Written by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/dashboard?tab=bugbot) for commit 44bde7b559b0fa1f056ddfa188f51b118d03c901. Configure [here](https://cursor.com/dashboard?tab=bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Action completed."}],"structuredContent":{"issues":[{"url":"https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2993","title":"fix(checkpoint): cap the legacy prompt_attributions carry-forward","issue_number":2993,"body":"`Metadata.LegacyPromptAttributions` is dead data — no CLI version computes, reads or sets it, and the field survives only so that rewriting an old checkpoint does not strip what entire.io still reads. But its carry-forward has no exit. Every path that re-emits a session's `metadata.json` decodes the whole `Metadata` and re-encodes it, so an oversized value an older CLI recorded is copied into a fresh blob on each rewrite — for the life of the session, and regardless of whether the rewrite had anything to do with attribution. A summary backfill re-commits it. So does a transcript finalize, a skill-events replacement, and a compact-transcript marker update.

That matters because this is the one metadata field whose size scales with the working tree rather than with the session. CLI versions before v0.10.1 recorded every file of every nested git checkout on every prompt, which is what produced the 70MB and 106MB `metadata.json` blobs that made `entire/checkpoints/v1` unpushable to GitHub. The per-blob hard limit there is 100 MiB, and one blob over it strands every checkpoint behind it on the branch — transcript and summary included.

So this caps the field at 4 MiB on the way through, and drops it past that rather than truncating it. Losing one opaque field is the cheaper loss.

## The cap is structural, not per-call-site

The git store had three separate places that marshalled a session `metadata.json` into a blob, and `updateSessionMetadata`'s three mutators sat behind one of them. Capping at the one site where the field is read forward would have left the other two re-committing it, so this adds `treeWriter.writeSessionMetadataBlob` as the single choke point all of them now go through, and the cap lives there. That costs threading `ctx` into `updateSessionMetadata`, `replaceSkillEvents` and `setCompactTranscriptStart`; every call site already had one in scope.

`ctx` has to be the caller's real context rather than `context.Background()`, or the drop is unexplainable afterwards: `logging` falls back to `slog.Default()` when the context carries no logger, nothing calls `slog.SetDefault` in production, and the warning would print to hook stderr instead of reaching `.entire/logs`.

The reference `fsstore` backend gets the same cap in its own carry-forward. That backend is test-only, but its contract says it mirrors the git store's per-session metadata semantics through the shared helpers, and the attribution carry-forward is one of the behaviours it deliberately reproduces.

## Why 4 MiB, and why only this field

Measured over this repo's own `entire/checkpoints/v1` history — 11,929 `metadata.json` blobs readable in this clone, of which only 11 exceed 64 KiB:

| field | largest value found |
| --- | --- |
| `prompt_attributions` | 1,810,321 bytes (1.73 MiB) |
| `initial_attribution` | 254 bytes |

4 MiB therefore clears every healthy record here by more than a factor of two, and fires only on the pathological shape above. `initial_attribution` is deliberately left uncapped: it is one snapshot per session rather than one per prompt, and at 254 bytes it is not a bloat vector — capping it would be ceremony.

## What this does not do

It does not repair the blobs already in history. A repo still carrying a 70–106 MiB `metadata.json` on its v1 branch stays unpushable, and fixing that needs the separate `doctor` scan-and-shrink that #2404 proposed. This is the prevention half only, rebased onto the field as it exists after the attribution removal (#2692) — #2404's own cap sits on a write path that no longer has a producer, so it would guard nothing today.

It also does not rewrite a slot nothing else touched. Attaching a second session leaves the first session's blob untouched, so there is nothing to re-emit and nothing to cap; that slot's field goes when the slot itself is next written. `TestRewritesDropOversizedLegacyPromptAttributions` pins that distinction rather than leaving it implied.

## Testing

`mise run check` (fmt, lint, test:ci). Each new test was mutation-checked rather than trusted: with the cap reverted, all three re-emission subtests fail while the untouched-slot subtest still passes, and narrowing `<=` to `<` makes the at-the-cap boundary case fail.

Stacked on #2844 (base branch `peyton/cross-repo-agent-commit-link`).

## Problem

In #2844, a checkpoint an agent's commit writes in another repository (B) keeps only the transcript up to the commit. Local mid-turn checkpoints are finalized at turn end with the full prompt-to-stop transcript; B's were not, so they miss everything after the commit, such as the agent's final reply.

## Change

- Condensing a foreign commit records the checkpoint and B's worktree in the home session's state (`ForeignTurnCheckpoints`, same lifecycle as `TurnCheckpointIDs`).
- At turn end, the home's hook runs `entire hooks git finalize-foreign --session … --home … --deadline … <ids>` (new hidden command) in each B, with repo-selecting git variables scrubbed and the process tree killed at the turn-end deadline. Running in B means B's settings, checkpoint store, image externalization and redaction apply, as they did at the commit. The child reads the home state read-only and only writes checkpoints that hold the session.
- Failures are logged and kept for a repeated turn end; turn start clears them. An interrupted finalize counts as a failure. The home's transcript start advances to the turn end only when every foreign checkpoint was finalized (even if the home also has its own mid-turn checkpoints), so a failure leaves the tail in the home's next checkpoint.
- If Entire is disabled in B by then, the command fails instead of reporting success.

## Tests

- Unit: finalize-foreign rewrites B's checkpoint with the later transcript, never writes the home state, refuses an unknown session and a checkpoint that doesn't hold the session; turn end groups per repository, keeps failures, retries only those.
- Integration (real git hooks, real subprocess): after A's turn end, B's checkpoint transcript has the reply written after the commit.

## What Copilot changed

Copilot CLI no longer puts `outputTokens` on `assistant.message`. Starting with 1.0.94, it writes a `session.usage_record` for each API call (main agent and subagents) instead. The record carries `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens` and `reasoningTokens`, and joins to its message by `apiCallId`. Local sessions from 1.0.83 through 1.0.93 have neither field, and 1.0.63 and earlier have only `outputTokens`. As a result, every checkpoint from a current Copilot session recorded zero tokens.

## Audit

| Path | Verdict | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `copilotcli.CalculateTokenUsage`, sliced read | Wrong for the new format: it reads only `assistant.message.outputTokens`, which no longer exists, so the result is 0 | Sum `session.usage_record` within the slice, and keep `outputTokens` as the fallback |
| `copilotcli.CalculateTokenUsage`, full read with `session.shutdown` | Wrong on every version. `inputTokens` includes cache read and write (Copilot's own `tokenDetails.input` equals input − cacheRead − cacheWrite), so cached input was counted twice. Only the last shutdown was read, but a resumed session writes one per run: per-run on 1.0.3 and cumulative on 1.0.97 | Normalized to fresh input. Each shutdown is classified by its request count, which matches the `assistant.message` count it covers on every release seen: the run's messages for a per-run shutdown, every message so far for a cumulative one. A run whose calls all have records is counted from the records. A shutdown that matches neither reading is ignored |
| `agentimport` Copilot importer | Delegates to the calculator, so it inherited the zero counts | Fixed through the calculator; comment updated |
| `compact` Copilot `output_tokens` | Empty on the new format | Joins `session.usage_record` by `apiCallId` and sets `output_tokens` plus fresh `input_tokens`, matching Claude's compact lines |
| `strategy` session-total backfill | Correct. It runs a full read at condensation, so it picks up the fix | No change; test added |
| Copilot hook payloads | No token fields | n/a |
| `AGENT.md` | Described the old format only | Rewritten with the observed format facts |

Confirmed on live 1.0.94 and 1.0.97 sessions: `reasoningTokens` is a subset of `outputTokens`, and `cacheWriteTokens` maps to `CacheCreationTokens`. The per-turn sums of `usage_record` equal the `session.shutdown` totals exactly, so checkpoint totals now add up to the session total. Subagent calls are counted in the main totals, and `SubagentTokens` stays unset as before.

## Tests

- `usage_record_test.go`, using a scrubbed 1.0.94 capture: each slice holds only its own calls, the slices sum to the normalized shutdown total, a full read before shutdown gives the same total, and a sliced read ignores the shutdown.
- A scrubbed 1.0.97 resumed session where the second shutdown is cumulative. A full read must equal the record sum (64/151364/23237/898/8), with and without the records, and the slices must add up to it.
- Tests for per-run shutdowns as on 1.0.3, a shutdown matching neither reading, mixed formats (no double counting), and input clamping.
- Compact, import and backfill tests for the new format.
- `TestCalculateTokenUsage_SessionShutdown` and `_MultiModel` pinned the inclusive input values (64807 and 1500). They now expect the fresh values, 22082 and 1150.

## Why

CLI versions before v0.10.1 walked nested git checkouts (Claude Code's `.claude/worktrees/`) into `prompt_attributions.user_added_per_file` on every prompt, producing 70MB and 106MB per-session `metadata.json` blobs on `entire/checkpoints/v1`. GitHub refuses blobs over 100 MiB, so one such blob anywhere in the branch history makes it unpushable and unmirrorable there. A customer hit exactly this (Plain T-88, Gitea push-mirrored to GitHub). The v0.10.1 fix (#1937, #1969) stopped new bloat but left the history behind, and the only remedy was a hand-written `git filter-repo` script.

## What

**Prevention.** `checkpoint.CapPromptAttributions` drops the field above 4 MiB at the checkpoint write boundary, in both writers. Nothing in the CLI reads the field back, and entire-api's ingest already salvages a `metadata.json` clipped at it.

**Repair.** `entire doctor` gains a "Checkpoint metadata size" check:
- scans the local branch and, when something is oversized, the elected sync remote's tracking ref (refreshed only then, so routine doctor runs stay offline);
- offers to rewrite the branch dropping the field from the oversized files, then force-push with `--force-with-lease` against the tip observed during the scan;
- preserves messages, authors, dates, `Encoding`/`ExtraHeaders`, checkpoint IDs and every other blob; history before the first oversized blob keeps its hashes; commits are re-signed when signing is configured.

**Safety decisions.**
- `doctor --force` does **not** apply this fix. It rewrites history and writes to a remote, and `--force` is run routinely by scripts and the e2e harness. The opt-in is an interactive yes or the new `entire doctor shrink-checkpoint-metadata [--yes]`.
- Local is rewritten **before** the remote is reconciled, with one memoized rewriter, so shared commits map to identical rewritten commits. The first draft reconciled the original local tip against the rewritten remote, which would have replayed every commit since the bloat as a duplicate; the adversarial review caught it and a test now pins the scenario.
- Rewritten tips are compared by **tree**, not hash: an independently repaired clone (or commit signing, which makes rewritten hashes differ) is adopted rather than replayed as no-op duplicates. Only genuine divergence falls through to `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef`.
- A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` URL is report-only: there is no tracking ref to lease against and pre-push's replay onto that URL would undo a local-only rewrite.
- `filemode.Deprecated` metadata files are treated as regular files in both scan and rewrite.
- The repair is per clone: another clone still holding the bloated branch replays it onto the repaired remote on its next push (`fetchAndRebaseRefCommon`), so the output says to run it in every clone.

Branch backend only; with git-refs primary the v1 branch is not what gets pushed.

## Tests

- `strategy`: scan finds only blobs over threshold; rewrite touches only affected commits, keeps transcripts byte-identical and is idempotent; force-push to a bare remote and recovery of remote-only bloat; **remote ahead by a new checkpoint yields each checkpoint exactly once**; an independent same-content rewrite is adopted, not replayed; `Deprecated` file mode handled; `stripPromptAttributions` unit.
- `cli`: clean repo is quiet; non-interactive run reports and names the subcommand; `runSessionsFix(cmd, true)` leaves the branch untouched; the subcommand with `--yes` rewrites and a second run finds nothing.
- New `testutil.CommitFiles` builds commits from a path→content map without a worktree.

Verified locally: build, vet, and golangci-lint 2.13.2 (via `go run`; the installed binary predates Go 1.27) on the touched packages report only the pre-existing unused `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` in `login.go`. All assertions pass. On this Windows machine every git-backed test, including untouched ones and the untouched `settings` package, fails only on `TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: ... .git: being used by another process`, so `mise run check` could not be run to green here; relying on CI for the full suite and the integration/canary runs.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Pre-push could strip oversized metadata from local-only commits before replaying them, making convergence automatic across clones instead of per-clone.
- Fresh Claude Code worktrees (`--worktree`, Remote Control worktree mode) contain no Entire config unless `.entire/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.json` are committed, so sessions there produce no checkpoints and commits get no trailer. Worth a doctor/status warning.

Hidden test tooling for evaluating the **git-refs** checkpoint store against real branch data: it re-materializes every checkpoint on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch as a per-checkpoint ref by re-driving the git-refs store's write path. Independent of the (still-undecided) byte-identical migration — standalone off `main`.

## What it does
`entire doctor rewrite-checkpoints` (hidden). For each checkpoint on the v1 branch:
- Replays each session's transcript through `Write`, so the compact `transcript.jsonl` is **regenerated**, the tree is **rooted at the checkpoint** (no shard folders), and `SessionFilePaths`/`CompactTranscriptStart` are correct by construction.
- Replays per-session summaries and combined attribution; grafts any `tasks/` subtree in unchanged.
- **Preserves the checkpoint id**, and **each commit keeps the original author** — read from the v1-branch commit that wrote the session (metadata carries no author), falling back to the repo git author.
- Fresh commits copy the data; the branch's own commits are not reused.

It writes refs **locally and does not push** (test tooling for now). Idempotent: existing refs are skipped unless `--force`; `--dry-run` reports without writing.

## Testing
`rewrite_test.go` (self-contained): root-flat layout + reads back via the git-refs store, author preserved from the branch commit, idempotency + `--force`, multi-session replay, dry-run/no-branch. Build clean, lint 0, checkpoint + cli suites pass.

## Notes
- Hidden from help — it's evaluation tooling, not a supported migration, while the migration approach is still being decided.
- Summary/attribution *backfill* commits use the repo author (consistent with the branch store's own backfills); only the session commits carry the original author.
- `transcript.jsonl` regeneration is best-effort (same as native git-refs writes) — produced when the transcript is compactable.

## What

Restores the git-refs-primary → v1-branch checkpoint fallback that is currently RED on `main` (blocks every PR):

`TestRunExplainAuto_GeneratePersistsHexOnBranchUnderRefsPrimary` fails with
`failed to save summary: fetch checkpoint ref ...: probe checkpoint ref ... on ://origin: git ls-remote: exit status 128`.

## Why

Under a git-refs primary, saving a summary for a pre-migration checkpoint that lives only on the v1 branch resolves the checkpoint through the git-refs store, which triggers an on-demand fetch of the missing ref. When the repo has **no origin remote and no configured `checkpoint_remote`**, fetch-target resolution falls back to the bare `"origin"` name, `git ls-remote origin` fails (exit 128), and `FetchCheckpointRef` returned that as a **hard error**.

Commit `7bbdad09c` ("git-refs: don't mask real errors as not-found") made `resolveRefMaybeFetch` propagate fetch failures instead of masking them as not-found — correct for genuine offline/network loss, but it also turned the no-remote probe failure into a hard error. That aborts the kind-routing `Write` backfill at the `ErrCheckpointNotFound` check (routing_store.go) instead of falling through to the v1-branch store, so the summary is discarded.

## How

The fix is localized to the fetch boundary and preserves `7bbdad09c`'s intent by distinguishing **no-remote** from **genuine-error**:

- `checkpointFetchTarget` now also reports `resolved` — whether a concrete fetch URL/remote was resolved at all. It is `false` **only** when URL resolution produced nothing (no origin, no `checkpoint_remote`, unreadable settings) and we fell back to the bare `"origin"` name.
- `FetchCheckpointRef`: when the ls-remote probe fails **and the target was that unresolved fallback**, it wraps `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`. The git-refs store maps that to `ErrCheckpointNotFound`, and routing falls back to the v1-branch store — mirroring `BranchExistsOnRemote`, which already treats an ls-remote failure as "not found".
- A genuine transport failure against a **resolved** remote (real origin URL or configured checkpoint remote) still propagates unchanged, and genuine absence still reads not-found.

- New: `TestFetchCheckpointRef_NoConfiguredRemoteIsAbsence` pins the "no configured remote → not-found → fallback" classification (the mirror of the unreachable-remote case).

## Motivation

Live incident (2026-08-12): a stray `git init` in a user's `$HOME` (no `.gitignore`) meant every agent Stop hook ran a worktree status walk over the entire home directory. The hook hung >120s; Claude Code stopped waiting at its ~60s hook timeout, but the `entire hooks claude-code stop` **process survived** — two zombies were found hours later at ~1.8GB RSS each, one with 25 CPU-minutes, still writing loose objects (200k+ files) into the repo. The failure was completely silent: no session state, no checkpoint, no log line — the session looked tracked. Trail finding `019ff792-3b10-72af-96d1-ddb7a7874064` on the feat/global-invisible trail documents it; this PR is the fix. The hazard exists on main today for any enabled repo with pathological status cost; global enable amplifies it by lazily enrolling uncurated repos.

## Fix shape

go-git's `Worktree.Status()` (the single sanctioned call site in `gitrepo/status.go`) is **not context-cancellable**, so the budget is a goroutine+select wrapper, `gitrepo.StatusWithBudget`:

- **20s wall-clock budget** (`gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget`): far beyond any healthy repo's walk, while leaving the remaining ~40s of the agent's ~60s hook timeout for the rest of the capture path (transcript copy, tree building, state writes) so the hook exits instead of being orphaned. No new user-facing setting.
- **On breach**: the walk goroutine is abandoned (it dies with the one-shot hook process — that is the point; a `recover` guard keeps an orphaned walk from crashing the hook if the caller closes the repo under it), and the returned error wraps the sentinel `gitrepo.ErrStatusBudgetExceeded`. Context cancellation is treated the same way — it arms the latch and carries the sentinel (with `ctx.Err()` still in the chain) — so a walk abandoned by cancellation cannot fail the hook hard or defeat the fail-open guarantee.
- **Actionable Warn** at breach names the repo root, elapsed, budget, and consequence ("capture degraded: untracked/new file detection skipped this turn") so `doctor logs` investigation finds it. Operational metadata only.
- **Zombie prevention**: a process-local latch makes every later `StatusWithBudget` call in the same hook process fail fast — the turn-start hook walks twice (pre-prompt capture + prompt attribution), and re-entering the walk after a breach is exactly what kept the incident processes alive.
- **The C-git half of the zombie**: the first-checkpoint path in the checkpoint store runs `git status --porcelain -z -uall` as a subprocess with no deadline, so after a go-git breach the hook could still get stuck in a child git instead of a goroutine. That subprocess is now bounded by the same `StatusWalkBudget` via `context.WithTimeout` (`exec.CommandContext` kills the child on expiry) and reports the same sentinel; the lifecycle handlers recognize it and warn-and-skip the checkpoint instead of failing the hook.

## Call sites bounded (agent-hook paths)

- `DetectFileChanges` (turn-end, subagent-end, Claude PostTodo) — errors were already Warn-and-continue.
- Pre-prompt / pre-task untracked scans (`CapturePrePromptState` / `CapturePreTaskState`) — these previously **failed the hook** on status error; they now fail open (hooks must never break the agent) and record an `UntrackedScanSkipped` marker in the state file.
- Prompt-attribution walk in `calculatePromptAttributionAtStart` — already fully fail-open; now also fails fast via the latch after a pre-prompt breach.
- First-checkpoint `git status` subprocess in `checkpoint/ephemeral.go` (`collectChangedFiles`), reached via `SaveStep` — bounded as above; `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` treats the sentinel from a save as warn-and-skip (hook exits 0), and its turn-end tail (LastPrompt backfill, phase transition, pre-prompt cleanup) still runs on that degrade path. The matching branch in `handleLifecycleSubagentEnd` is defensive symmetry, not a live path: task saves write via `writeTask`, which reads no worktree status today. The go-git walk budget and this C-git budget deliberately stack (~40s worst case of the ~60s hook timeout) rather than sharing the breach latch — C git is much faster and honors ignores, so it often produces a real first checkpoint where the go-git walk breached, and unlike the walk it is reliably killed on expiry.

Left unbounded deliberately: `checkCanRewindWithWarning` (rewind machinery, no CLI surface), review-worktree removal, and `entire session adopt` — a user is actively waiting on those commands, they are not hook paths, and a slow-but-healthy repo (NFS, cold cache) should finish rather than error at the budget. Adopt originally inherited the budget through `DetectFileChanges`; it now uses an explicit unbounded variant (`detectFileChangesUnbounded`) so the budget stays a hook-path property. Git-hook paths (post-commit condensation) never call Status.

## Degradation semantics

On breach, capture proceeds with transcript-derived files. New-file detection is skipped for the turn: the `UntrackedScanSkipped` marker tells turn-end/subagent-end to drop `changes.New`, because without a pre-prompt baseline every untracked file in the worktree would be misattributed to the agent. This matters precisely in the cross-process shape — turn start breaches (marker written), turn end runs in a fresh process whose walk succeeds — and is covered by dedicated tests that fail if either guard is removed. Modified/deleted detection degrades to nil alongside the status error, as before. A breach inside the save itself (the C-git first-checkpoint read) skips that checkpoint with a Warn and still exits 0.

One deliberate widening beyond the budget feature: the pre-prompt/pre-task untracked scans now fail open on **any** error (repo-open failure, corrupted `.git`, …), not just budget breaches. Previously any status error there failed the TurnStart/SubagentStart hook and broke the agent's turn; that fail-hook behavior was the bug — the scan only feeds new-file detection, so the correct degrade is warn + marker + transcript-derived capture. The code comment at `untrackedFilesOrSkip` states this explicitly.

Degradation is visible outside `.entire/logs`: turn end persists `SessionState.CaptureDegradedAt` when any status scan feeding the turn breached (marker, `DetectFileChanges` sentinel, or a breach inside the save), and clears it on the next healthy turn. `entire status` prints a per-session warning ("capture degraded …: status scan over budget; new-file detection skipped") and `entire status --json` carries `capture_degraded` on the session brief, so a repo that breaches every turn no longer reports a healthy session while new-file detection is silently off.

## Tests

- `TestStatusWithBudget_BreachAbandonsWalkPromptly` — breach surfaces the sentinel at the budget (not when the walk ends) and the latch stops a second walk from starting; pins the zombie regression.
- `TestStatusWithBudget_BreachWarnsWithRepoRoot` — the breach Warn carries the `repo_root` attribute (the incident was silent; this pins the observability).
- `TestTurnFlow_StatusBudgetBreachDegradesGracefully` — same-process shape: full turn-start + turn-end with the latch set; both hooks return success and the checkpoint contains the transcript-derived file.
- `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_ScanSkippedMarkerSkipsNewFileDetection` / `TestHandleLifecycleSubagentEnd_ScanSkippedMarkerSkipsNewFileDetection` — cross-process shape: marker written under a breach, end-hook walk succeeds; the checkpoint must not claim pre-existing untracked files. Verified by mutation: deleting either `changes.New` guard fails the corresponding test.
- `TestCollectChangedFiles_BudgetExceededReturnsSentinel` — the first-checkpoint `git status` subprocess had no deadline and could outlive the agent's hook timeout; on expiry the error must wrap `gitrepo.ErrStatusBudgetExceeded` so the lifecycle warn-and-skip path recognizes it.
- `TestStatusWithBudget_CancellationArmsLatchAndCarriesSentinel` — a walk abandoned by context cancellation must degrade like a timer breach (sentinel carried, latch armed) while `context.Canceled` stays in the error chain.
- `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_SaveBreachStillBackfillsLastPrompt` — a breach inside the save must still run the turn-end tail: checkpoint skipped, hook exits 0, LastPrompt backfilled, `CaptureDegradedAt` persisted.
- The marker tests above also pin `CaptureDegradedAt` being set on a degraded turn and cleared by the next healthy one.

## Why

The `checkpoint_version` stamp in each checkpoint's root `metadata.json` was a pure label: which storage backend serves a checkpoint is decided by the settings topology, and nothing ever dispatched on the stored value. The `EnsureCanReadVersion` read gates at resume/explain/rewind/export were forward-compat tripwires that could only fire for checkpoint formats that never shipped. Both are dead complexity — every reader had to thread a version through code that had exactly one possible answer.

Existing checkpoints' stored `checkpoint_version` values are handled by an external migration, so no backward-compat handling for the stored attribute is needed here.

## What changed

Removed the read gates first (they read the field), then the field itself: `WriteOptions.CheckpointVersion`, `CheckpointSummary.CheckpointVersion`, the stamping plumbing through the write chain, the read-side backfill (`normalizeCheckpointSummary`), and the now-unused `CheckpointVersionRefsV1` constant. Two follow-up cleanups: the hidden `entire checkpoint policy` help text now describes `checkpoint_version` as a write guard rather than a format selector, and the branch↔refs seam test regained a primary-read discriminator.

## Decisions made during development

- **The checkpoint policy subsystem is intentionally untouched.** Its `checkpoint_version` field remains a checkpoint-data write guard (`CanSatisfyPolicy`): a repo can still block writes from CLIs that don't support the configured version. It just no longer feeds a stamp into new summaries. `attach` switched from the deleted `checkpointVersionForNewCheckpoint` to the shared `ensureCheckpointPolicyAllowsCheckpointData` gate that explain and import already use.
- **`CheckpointVersionBranchV1` stays** — it anchors the policy defaults (`DefaultPolicy`, `Normalize`); only the refs-v1 constant became unused.
- **The seam test needed a new probe.** Dropping the version assert removed the only signal distinguishing a read served by the git-refs primary from one served by the git-branch mirror. The test now deletes the mirror's v1 branch and asserts the composed store still serves full reads — something only the primary can do.

## Reviewer notes

- Existing checkpoints and existing policy refs are left as-is; the stored-field cleanup ships as an external migration.
- Commits are ordered to be reviewable independently (gates → field → help text → seam test) and can be split into a stack if preferred.

## Why

`session adopt` moves a live session into the current worktree and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping (`StepCount`, `CheckpointTranscriptStart`, `LastCheckpointID`, and `FilesTouched`). Selecting the wrong session can therefore mutate another agent's running session and detach its next commit from its work.

That happened when an agent read a foreign session ID from `entire session current` and passed it to `session adopt`. #2322 made caller resolution explicit through `SessionResolution` and `IsCaller()`; this PR applies that ownership boundary to the command that mutates a session.

The existing checks were insufficient:

- `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` only proves the session ID and source worktree agree with each other.
- `isAdoptableSourceSession` only proves the session is still live.

Neither proves that the selected session belongs to the process invoking the command.

## Behavior

| Case | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The selected session is identified as the caller's own | Adopt silently |
| A different session is identified as the caller | Require terminal confirmation; refuse without a terminal |
| Caller ownership is ambiguous, unavailable, or based on an incomplete candidate set | Require terminal confirmation; refuse without a terminal |
| `--allow-foreign-session` is passed | Proceed deliberately |

Auto-selection uses the same guard, so `entire session adopt --from <path>` cannot bypass ownership checks by omitting the session ID. The ownership decision is repeated against the locked source state immediately before mutation.

Non-interactive refusal prints an actionable `--allow-foreign-session` remedy. Prompt cancellation follows the shared form-cancellation path and cannot proceed with the mutation.

## Combined caller resolution

Cross-repository adoption cannot rely on the ordinary resolver alone: `ResolveCallerSession` reads the current repository's session store, while the relevant owner may exist only in the source store. This matters for Gemini CLI and OpenCode, which publish no caller-session environment variable and can only be identified through process ancestry.

`IdentifyCallerSession` therefore runs the identification tier over the combined target and source candidate set. Source states are first-class candidates rather than a fallback, and supplied source state wins an ID collision with a stale target copy. The shared resolver remains the single ownership policy:

- nearest owner in process ancestry wins;
- equal ancestry depth is broken by most recent interaction;
- inherited environment claims do not outrank a nearer recorded owner;
- the existing depth-zero rule applies when an unplaceable claim cannot be nearer;
- imported and already-adopted states do not compete;
- ambiguity does not authorize mutation.

## Incomplete candidate sets

A store listing normally skips an individual state file it cannot read so one corrupt file does not hide every healthy session. That is appropriate for display, but unsafe for ownership: a missing candidate may be the nearer owner whose absence changes the winner.

`StateStore.ListWithSkipped` reports those omissions and `ResolvedSession.Incomplete` carries them through caller resolution. Adoption fails closed when either source or target candidates are incomplete, while `session list`, `session current`, and both `session tokens` selection paths warn on stderr and keep structured stdout valid.

The detailed invariants and rejected alternatives are documented in [`docs/architecture/session-caller-resolution.md`](docs/architecture/session-caller-resolution.md).

## Why the override is separate

`--allow-foreign-session` is intentionally distinct from `--force` and `--yes`. Those flags already control replacement and same-store confirmation, and agents commonly retry failures with `--force`. Waiving ownership requires a flag that states that intent explicitly.

## Tests

Comprehensive unit and real-binary integration coverage includes:

- foreign, unidentified, and ambiguous callers;
- successful adoption of the caller's own session;
- cross-repository agents without a session-ID environment variable;
- nested owners, inherited environment claims, and equal-depth recency;
- source/target ID collisions and source-state precedence;
- locked ownership revalidation;
- incomplete source and target stores;
- `--force` / `--yes` not granting the waiver;
- `--allow-foreign-session` registration and behavior;
- non-interactive refusal output and preservation of source state;
- completeness warnings for session list/current/tokens without corrupting JSON output.

Existing adoption tests identify their fixture through `adoptAsCaller`, so they exercise the supported path rather than the escape hatch and remain isolated from caller-session variables inherited from a developer's agent.

## Validation

- `mise run lint`
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/ ./cmd/entire/cli/strategy/`
- `go test -tags=integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test -run 'TestSessionAdoptGuard_' -count=1`
- `GOOS=windows go vet ./cmd/...`

### Existing macOS-only failures

Four unrelated tests fail on clean `origin/main` because macOS resolves `/var/...` to `/private/var/...` while their expected strings use the unresolved `t.TempDir()` path:

- `TestCheckAgentDirSymlinks_ScansBeneathAVouchedLink`
- `REDACTED`
- `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_UsesTheQuotedCommand`
- `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_RemedyIsPasteable`

They are unchanged by this PR.

Makes the OpenCode integration work on OpenCode 2 while keeping OpenCode 1 working from the same generated plugin. Fixes #2588.

OpenCode 2 is a hard break in two places:

1. It loads a default plugin definition with `id` + `setup`/`effect`, and rejects V1 hook-map plugins with `PluginModule.LoadError: Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function`.
2. It moved export/import under `opencode session`; the V1 `opencode export` prints a help page and exits 0.

This builds on the approach in #2397 (thanks @aryasaatvik) but keeps OpenCode 1 plugin support instead of dropping it.

## Changes

**Plugin** (`entire_plugin.ts` + committed dogfood copy)
- Default export `{ id: "entire", setup(ctx) }` for OpenCode 2: `session.hook("prompt")` drives turn-start, `session.hook("context")` applies the turn-start context injection and tracks the model, and `ctx.event.subscribe()` handles `session.created`, `session.idle`/`session.status`/`session.execution.*`, `session.compacted`, `session.deleted`, `global.disposed`, `location.shutdown`.
- Keeps the named `EntirePlugin` export (older V1) and adds a `server()` factory on the default export (V1 ≥ 1.18.29).
- No runtime dependency on either SDK package (the V1 type import was removed), so the file loads under Bun and Node with no project `node_modules`.

**Commands** (`cli_commands.go`)
- Try `opencode session export` / `session import` first, fall back to the V1 top-level commands.
- Validate export output, so an exit-0 help page is not treated as a transcript, and preserve a classified V2 error across the fallback.

**Schema** (`types.go`, `transcript.go`, `transcript/compact/opencode.go`)
- Normalize OpenCode 2's flattened messages (`type` + `content`, message-level `text`) to the v1 model for reads, while keeping the raw transcript byte-preserving so `opencode session import` can resume the session.

**e2e**
- Accept `opencode v2.x` version output and skip V1 plugin-dependency seeding on major ≥ 2.

**Docs** — agent guide updated for both plugin APIs and both export commands.

## Verification

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/... ./e2e/agents/...` clean.
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/... ./cmd/entire/cli/transcript/...` pass, including the new `opencode_v2_test.go` schema/export tests and a Node canary that drives the V2 `setup` path (session-start, turn-start, turn-end) alongside the existing V1 canary.
- Loaded the generated plugin against real **OpenCode 2.0.16**: the server logs `loading plugin` with no subsequent `failed to load plugin`.
- Confirmed the command split on 2.0.16: `opencode session export <id>` returns session JSON; `opencode export <id>` prints `DESCRIPTION`/`USAGE` and exits 0.

## Notes

- The V2 event subscription guards turn-end with a `turnActive` flag, because OpenCode 2 can report a turn ending via more than one event.

`SanitizePathForCursor` builds the name of Cursor's project directory (`~/.cursor/projects/<name>`) from the repo path, but not the way Cursor does. Cursor collapses runs of non-alphanumeric characters into one `-` and trims `-` from both ends; Entire only stripped the leading `/` and replaced each character separately. Any path with two separators in a row (a `.worktrees` checkout, `/-…` segments) or any Windows path (`C:\…` → `C--…`) got a directory Cursor never writes to.

Everything Entire computes from that directory is then wrong: resume restores a transcript where Cursor never reads it, attach and history import look in the wrong place, transcript discovery misses the session, and a transcript under Cursor's real directory isn't recognised as Cursor's. Cursor's hooks send `transcript_path: null` until the transcript file exists, so on a session's first turn the turn start computes the path, and the wrong one stays in session state until the next hook carries the real path.

On this machine, Entire's rule names 60 of the 78 Cursor project directories correctly (from their `.workspace-trusted` files); all 18 misses are worktrees or `--` paths. Windows paths are affected too (`C:\repo` → `C--repo`, Cursor uses `C-repo`).

ASCII-only, case kept. It matches all 78 directories on this machine.
- History import's repo-boundary walk (`pathsWithEncoding`, which refuses transcripts whose project directory another repo also maps to) assumed one output character per path character. With collapsing and trimming, a directory can encode to nothing or to the target itself and still lead to a match, so the walk now descends into those too. It stays fail-closed: if the walk hits its read limit, the transcript is treated as shared and not imported.
- Comments that said "the CLI sends a null transcript_path" now say it's null until the transcript exists, in both the IDE and the CLI.

No fallback to the old naming: Cursor never wrote under it, so nothing on disk depends on it. Resume now writes into the directory Cursor actually reads (still guarded by the existing-log check and `--force`).

## Tests

- Sanitizer table with collapsing, trimming, Windows, worktree and case rows; a parity table whose expected values come from running Cursor's own function (empty, `/`, `-`, `/a/`, non-ASCII letters, emoji, NUL, `C:\x`, `C:/x`).

- First turn: a repo under `<tmp>/a/.worktrees/repo`, the transcript where Cursor writes it, and a `stop` with `transcript_path: null` resolves to that file.

## Summary

## What Copilot changed

Copilot CLI no longer puts `outputTokens` on `assistant.message`. Starting with 1.0.94, it writes a `session.usage_record` for each API call (main agent and subagents) instead. The record carries `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens` and `reasoningTokens`, and joins to its message by `apiCallId`. Local sessions from 1.0.83 through 1.0.93 have neither field, and 1.0.63 and earlier have only `outputTokens`. As a result, every checkpoint from a current Copilot session recorded zero tokens.

## Audit

| Path | Verdict | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `copilotcli.CalculateTokenUsage`, sliced read | Wrong for the new format: it reads only `assistant.message.outputTokens`, which no longer exists, so the result is 0 | Sum `session.usage_record` within the slice, and keep `outputTokens` as the fallback |
| `copilotcli.CalculateTokenUsage`, full read with `session.shutdown` | Wrong on every version. `inputTokens` includes cache read and write (Copilot's own `tokenDetails.input` equals input − cacheRead − cacheWrite), so cached input was counted twice. Only the last shutdown was read, but a resumed session writes one per run: per-run on 1.0.3 and cumulative on 1.0.97 | Normalized to fresh input. Each shutdown is classified by its request count, which matches the `assistant.message` count it covers on every release seen: the run's messages for a per-run shutdown, every message so far for a cumulative one. A run whose calls all have records is counted from the records. A shutdown that matches neither reading is ignored |
| `agentimport` Copilot importer | Delegates to the calculator, so it inherited the zero counts | Fixed through the calculator; comment updated |
| `compact` Copilot `output_tokens` | Empty on the new format | Joins `session.usage_record` by `apiCallId` and sets `output_tokens` plus fresh `input_tokens`, matching Claude's compact lines |
| `strategy` session-total backfill | Correct. It runs a full read at condensation, so it picks up the fix | No change; test added |
| Copilot hook payloads | No token fields | n/a |
| `AGENT.md` | Described the old format only | Rewritten with the observed format facts |

Confirmed on live 1.0.94 and 1.0.97 sessions: `reasoningTokens` is a subset of `outputTokens`, and `cacheWriteTokens` maps to `CacheCreationTokens`. The per-turn sums of `usage_record` equal the `session.shutdown` totals exactly, so checkpoint totals now add up to the session total. Subagent calls are counted in the main totals, and `SubagentTokens` stays unset as before.

## Tests

- `usage_record_test.go`, using a scrubbed 1.0.94 capture: each slice holds only its own calls, the slices sum to the normalized shutdown total, a full read before shutdown gives the same total, and a sliced read ignores the shutdown.
- A scrubbed 1.0.97 resumed session where the second shutdown is cumulative. A full read must equal the record sum (64/151364/23237/898/8), with and without the records, and the slices must add up to it.
- Tests for per-run shutdowns as on 1.0.3, a shutdown matching neither reading, mixed formats (no double counting), and input clamping.
- Compact, import and backfill tests for the new format.
- `TestCalculateTokenUsage_SessionShutdown` and `_MultiModel` pinned the inclusive input values (64807 and 1500). They now expect the fresh values, 22082 and 1150.

## Summary

Since #2692, a commit links to a session by the files the session recorded. Two cases recorded nothing when an agent changed a file through a shell command, so the commit carrying that file got no `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.

**Shell edit to a file that was already untracked.** Turn end excludes untracked files that existed at prompt start from "new", and git status cannot report an untracked file as modified, so the edit was invisible. The prompt-start baseline now also records each untracked file's stat data (`PrePromptState.UntrackedFileStats`): size, modification time, inode and status-change time, the fields git's index compares. The change time catches a same-size rewrite that restores the modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`); Windows has no change time, so only size and modification time are compared there. At turn end, a baseline file whose stat data changed joins the modified list before `filterToUncommittedFiles`, so a file committed mid-turn is still dropped. Stat data instead of content hashes keeps `UserPromptSubmit` free of an extra `git hash-object` per prompt.

**File created by a background subagent's shell command after the parent's turn ended.** A background SubagentStop deliberately skips the worktree scan (it would sweep in the parent's and other agents' concurrent work), and the transcript names no file. Once the parent's next prompt starts, the file sits in that prompt's untracked baseline, so no later turn end claims it. SubagentStop now also claims untracked files created since the task launched that no session in the same worktree has recorded (`unrecordedNewFilesSinceLaunch`). Files the parent's own turns or another session recorded are excluded. When another background task in the worktree overlapped this one (new `TaskRecord.Background` flag, still live or completed after this task's launch), nothing is claimed, since the first task to stop would otherwise take both tasks' files. Accepted trade-off: a file the user creates while the parent is idle is claimed as well. Since #2692 removed line attribution, that only adds a session link to the commit carrying it, which matches what turn end already does for user edits made during an active turn.

The first commit also pins the ordering from #2653: a background task completes mid-turn and the parent commits in the same turn. The commit links, lists the file, and carries the subagent transcript. #2653's reported symptom was in line attribution, which #2692 removed.

## Tests

- `TestSubagentCheckpoints_BackgroundTaskCompletesMidTurn_ParentCommitLinks`: the #2653 ordering. It fails if the subagent's completion is dropped.
- `TestShellEditToPreExistingUntrackedFile_LinksCommit`: the shell-edited file is recorded and linked, and an untouched pre-existing untracked file is not recorded.
- `TestBackgroundSubagentShellCreatedFile_LinksCommit`: the subagent's shell-created file is recorded and linked.
- `TestShellRewriteKeepingSizeAndMtime_IsRecorded`: a same-size rewrite with the original modification time restored is still recorded. Skipped on Windows. It fails when the change time is dropped from the comparison.
- `TestOverlappingBackgroundTasks_ClaimNoNewFiles`: two overlapping background tasks from different sessions each create a file, and neither session claims either file. It fails when the overlap check is removed.
- `REDACTED`: of five files, the task claims only the subagent's file and the user's idle-window file. It does not claim the pre-launch file, the parent's later-turn file, or another session's file. It fails when the "already recorded" exclusion is removed.

Both gap tests failed on main before the fix. Their controls, where the transcript names the file, passed.

`mise run check` passes.

Every agent's `DetectPresence` asks *"does `<repo>/.<agent>/` exist"*. That's a fair test for Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini, which all create repo-local config as a matter of course. It's structurally unfair to Cursor: project rules are optional, and Cursor's real per-project state lives in `~/.cursor/projects/<sanitized-repo-path>`.

So a repo driven daily from Cursor reports "not present". `entire enable` enables only detected agents when non-interactive, and pre-selects only detected ones on first run (`selectAgents`, `setup.go:1771-1795`). The observed result is worse than Cursor merely being skipped — enable falls back to the **default** agent, wires Claude Code, and prints "Ready.":

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| enable says | `Agent: Claude Code (use --agent to change)` | `Detected agent: Cursor` |
| `.cursor/hooks.json` | absent | 7 hooks |
| wired instead | `.claude/settings.json` | — |

A/B'd with real binaries in a fresh repo with `~/.cursor/projects/<repo>/` present and no repo-local `.cursor/`.

## Why this is load-bearing: the missing counterpart to #1262

#1262 reported this exact repo state — Claude Code hooks installed, `.cursor/hooks.json` absent, Cursor in use — and its consequence: the Cursor session was *claimed* by Claude's forwarded hooks and misattributed. `fadc4a06a` fixed that with `hook_guard.go`, which inspects the transcript path and makes the forwarded hook no-op when the session belongs to another agent.

That fix is correct, and it changes the failure mode for anyone in that state:

- **before** — Claude's forwarded hook claimed the session → sessions appeared under the wrong agent. Wrong, but visible.
- **after** — the guard correctly declines → nothing claims the session → **zero capture, silently**.

#1262 shipped one half. The guard stops the *wrong* agent from claiming a Cursor session; nothing ensured the *right* agent is wired to claim it. Users in that state went from misattributed sessions to correct attribution of nothing at all. This is that second half.

The user-visible symptom has been reported from outside more than once — #574 ("Unable to see agent steps on dashboard") and #898 ("empty Cursor session panel").

## What changed

`DetectPresence` keeps the repo-local check first and adds the state dir as a second signal. `GetSessionDir` and `DetectPresence` both resolve it through a new `projectStateDir` helper, so the two cannot disagree about where Cursor keeps a repo's state.

The second signal deliberately tolerates a false positive — a repo opened in Cursor once and never used with its agent. That installs hooks which never fire, which is harmless; a false negative captures nothing and says nothing.

## Verification

Cursor capture itself is healthy once hooks exist — `TestSingleSessionManualCommit` with `cursor-cli` passes on Cursor CLI `2026.08.11`, full lifecycle (`SessionStart` → `TurnStart` → `TurnEnd` → checkpoint saved → condensed), commit trailered `Entire-Checkpoint`, v1 checkpoint carrying `Entire-Agent: Cursor`. Detection was the only thing standing between a Cursor user and that path.

Four tests, two RED-verified (they fail with the second signal stubbed, pass with it). Tests set `HOME`/`USERPROFILE` to a temp dir so they never read the developer's real `~/.cursor`.

`initGitRepo` now runs a real `git init`: the hand-written `.git/HEAD` it created before is not a repo the git CLI accepts, so `paths.WorktreeRoot` failed with exit 128 on it — existing tests never noticed because `DetectPresence` falls back to CWD on that error. This package can't use `testutil.InitRepo`; `architecture_test.go` forbids agent packages from importing `cli` internals.

`mise run check` green.

## Not addressed here

Found while investigating, each worth its own issue: headless (`cursor-agent -p`) captures nothing at all because only `sessionStart`/`sessionEnd` fire so no session state is created — though the transcript *is* written to disk, so it's fixable from `sessionEnd`; Cursor has no `ContextInjector`, and `sessionStart`'s `additional_context` is verified working, so that's now viable; and nothing anywhere detects "hooks installed, never fired", which is the state every one of these leaves you in.

## Problem

Run one agent session that makes the changes, then a second session that just reviews the branch. The review session touches no files, but it gets condensed into the next checkpoint when the first session commits mid-turn.

Two paths in `shouldCondenseWithOverlapCheck` (`strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go`) let a session skip the file-overlap check: ACTIVE with recent interaction, and IDLE with a fresh task record. The only thing that stops a file-less session on those paths is the read-only gate: skip it if another session claims the committed files. A review session reaches the bypass through either shape, and the gate misses it.

## Fixes

1. **Only in-flight task records bypass the overlap check.** A background subagent that only reads files still gets a completed record at SubagentStop. That record was trusted exactly like an in-flight one, but a finished subagent cannot be the process committing, and completion already merged its files into `FilesTouched`. `idleWithTaskContent` becomes `idleWithLiveTaskRecord` and only considers `LiveTaskRecords()`. It still feeds the fast path, the trailer gate, and the condensation bypass, so the three stay one rule.
2. **Count mid-turn claimants.** The gate counted claimants from persisted `FilesTouched`, which a session committing mid-turn has not written yet (SaveStep runs at Stop). When no persisted claimant exists, `countMidTurnClaimants` checks ACTIVE sessions' live transcripts for committed files. It reads the transcript directly rather than `resolveFilesTouched`, which returns a stale earlier-turn list whenever one exists. An ordinary commit, where persisted `FilesTouched` already claims the files, pays no extra transcript parse.
3. **Don't drop a live subagent's co-author.** Arming the gate more often exposed a case it now got wrong: an IDLE session whose still-running background subagent edited part of the commit also has empty `FilesTouched`. Before dropping a live-record session as read-only, the gate reads its in-flight records' transcripts (declared path, then agent-layout fallback, as `materializeTaskRecords` does) for committed files. This runs lazily, only for a session the gate would otherwise drop.

## Behavior change

`AcceptsIdleSessionWithCompletedTaskRecord` pinned the old rule and is flipped to `Declines…`. The work it protected, a background subagent finishing with uncommitted edits that get committed later, still links through `FilesTouched`, and `REDACTED` pins that for both TTY and no-TTY commits, including the task transcript under `tasks/`.

## Tests

- `TestReviewSession_CodingSessionCommitsMidTurn_NotCondensed`: finished and running reviewer subtests; both failed before the fix.
- `TestReviewSession_FinishedReviewer_UnrelatedCommitNotLinked`: isolates fix 1 (no other claimant, so the gate never fires); fails with fix 1 reverted.

- `REDACTED`: completed-with-files records still link.

agy (Google Antigravity CLI) has had a `SessionStart` hook since 1.1.1. Our integration said it had none, so Entire never installed it. I checked this against the release binaries: the hook type is absent in 1.0.4–1.1.0 and present in 1.1.1, and `agy -p /hooks` loads a workspace SessionStart hook on 1.1.12, 1.2.10 and 1.3.4.

Without it, agy sessions never reach Entire's SessionStart handler, which is what starts the sweep that finalizes sessions whose agent process has exited. agy only ever sends TurnEnd, so every finished agy conversation sat idle until another agent started in the same repo, `entire doctor` ran, or the 7-day purge removed it.

This PR installs it the same way the other agents do (agent integration checklist and agent guide):

- **Hook verb:** `session-start`, first in `HookNames()`, so the hook runs `entire hooks antigravity session-start`.
- **Parsing:** shaped like Cursor's `parseSessionStart`. It uses `ReadAndParseHookInput`, so empty and malformed input are errors. The event carries SessionID = `conversationId`, SessionRef = `transcriptPath` and Model = `modelName`, so the model hint is stored as for Cursor and Claude Code.
- **Install:** the hook is written by the existing per-host builder, so the wrapper choice, `OpenHookConfig` and legacy-prefix handling are unchanged. Installs now write 4 hooks. An existing 3-hook entry is upgraded by any install, and foreign entries are kept.
- **No output:** no stdout, no banner, no injected context. agy has no user-only display field.
- **Doctor:** adding a hook would have made every existing install look "STALE FOR THIS HOST". `HooksEntryWrongHost` now flags only entries holding the other OS's wrapper.
- **Docs:** fixes the stale "no SessionStart surface" notes in AGENT.md, lifecycle.go and agent-guide.md, and adds Antigravity to the guide's event-mapping table.

### Live check (agy 1.3.4, isolated HOME, invalid API key, so no billed calls)

- **When it fires:** once per new conversation, before the first model call. In `-p` mode that's at startup; interactively it's at the first prompt, not when the app opens. It doesn't fire on `--conversation` resume.
- **Payload:** `conversationId`, `transcriptPath`, `workspacePaths`, `modelName`, `artifactDirectoryPath`.
- **Hook parent:** the agy process itself, in both modes, and it is gone after agy exits. So the owner-based sweep can finalize the session.
- **Stray output or failure:** non-JSON stdout or a nonzero exit is logged by agy as an error, and the run continues.

### Not verified

- **Older agy:** how releases before 1.1.1 treat the unknown `SessionStart` key. AGENT.md says this is unverified.
- **OAuth mode:** the e2e hook probe now expects SessionStart, so the next CI run checks it.
- **Follow-up:** the existing "resumes start at `invocationNum > 0`" note doesn't match agy 1.3.4, where a resumed conversation's first PreInvocation has `invocationNum` 0.

### Testing

`mise run check` passes. Tests cover:
- parsing all fields;
- empty and malformed input;
- the hook list;
- the install count and its Windows wrapper;
- upgrading a 3-hook entry while keeping foreign entries;
- `HooksEntryWrongHost`;
- doctor's wrong-host and outdated cases;
- the integration flow with session-start (stdout empty, model hint stored);
- the e2e probe's expected hooks.

## Problem

`entire status` had two defects in how it reports sessions, both fixed here.

**`--json` collapsed `active_sessions` to one entry per agent.** Two sessions for the same agent — one per worktree, a normal setup — showed as one, and nothing in the output let a consumer recover the second. The text path already listed every session, so the two surfaces disagreed.

**Reporting mutated what it reported.** Both paths read through `StateStore.List`, which deletes stale records as it reads, and both ran `finalizeExitedSessions`. Running the command people run to *look* at state changed that state: a stale session vanished because you looked at it, and a dead-owner session was finalized on read instead of being reported as exited.

## Summary

- add `StateStore.ListReadOnly` beside the existing mutating reads, splitting stale cleanup behind a parameter
- status reads read-only on both the text and JSON paths and finalizes nothing
- `--json` reports one entry per session, carrying `session_id`, `worktree_path`, and `branch`

`List` and `Load` keep their cleanup contract exactly as before — `entire doctor` and the session sweeper still call them and still finalize, verified by test.

## Behaviour changes worth calling out in review

1. **`active_sessions` JSON shape**: one entry per session instead of one per agent. Consumers grouping on `agent` still work; anything relying on exactly one entry per agent does not. The reverse was impossible — a collapsed entry could not be un-collapsed.
2. **Status no longer finalizes exited sessions.** A dead-owner session now shows as `exited` until `doctor` or the sweeper reaches it. `CLAUDE.md` and `sessions-and-checkpoints.md` both documented the old behaviour and are corrected here.

`TestRunStatusJSON_DeduplicatesSessions` pinned the old shape and is replaced by `TestRunStatusJSON_ReportsEachSessionSeparately` rather than deleted.

## Verification

- `mise run check` — unit, integration, and the Vogon canary, all green
- new: `TestStateStore_ListReadOnly_ReturnsStaleWithoutDeleting` asserts stale records survive a read *and* that `List` still deletes them
- new: `TestRunStatusJSON_ListsEverySessionWithoutMutating` — went red on both defects before the fix
- ported: `TestStatusMultipleSessionsPreservedAcrossWorktrees`, `TestStatusReadOnlyPreservesDeadOwnerStateAndTranscript` (asserts state file and transcript are byte- and mtime-identical after status)

Fixes #2362

Split out of #2343, which bundled this with unrelated Git-hook work.

Fixes #1890.

## Problem
A session records `SessionState.WorktreePath` once at start, and the commit-time
matcher (`findSessionsForWorktree`) uses exact string equality. When the repo
directory is renamed/moved while the session is stopped and the agent resumes it
(Claude Code's own `/resume`) from the new location, the recorded path no longer
resolves — every commit silently loses its `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. #1440's
sibling-worktree fallback doesn't cover a whole-repo move: the old path is gone,
so nothing matches.

## Fix
Reconcile on the resumed turn, **scoped to main-worktree relocations**. When a
turn starts and the recorded path no longer resolves to this repo's git common
dir, repoint `WorktreePath` at the current worktree — but only when the session
and the current worktree are both the **main** worktree (`WorktreeID == ""` on
both sides). The session store lives in the common dir, so a loaded state is the
same repo by construction; a recorded path that still resolves to this repo (a
live sibling worktree) is left untouched.

## Why main-worktree only
`WorktreeID` keys the session's shadow branch (`entire/<base>-hash(WorktreeID)`).
Repointing a **linked**-worktree session onto the main worktree while keeping its
`WorktreeID` would leave `WorktreeID` describing a different worktree than
`WorktreePath`. An audit of every `WorktreeID`/`WorktreePath` consumer showed that
disalignment is reachable by code that re-derives the worktree id from the current
directory instead of reading `state.WorktreeID`:

- `entire clean` (and its `--dry-run` preview) compute the wrong shadow-branch
  name → the session's real branch is orphaned.
- `entire explain` / rewind-point listing filter shadow branches by the current
  worktree hash → the session's checkpoints are hidden.
- post-commit base/attribution updates follow the wrong worktree's HEAD → skewed
  agent-vs-human attribution.

The reported case (#1890) is a whole main-checkout relocation, where `WorktreeID`
is `""` throughout — so restricting to that fixes the bug **without ever creating
the disaligned state**, and `WorktreePath`/`WorktreeID` stay aligned by
construction. Linked-worktree relocation is a rare, documented non-goal; the
zero-match path still warns so the trailer loss is not silent.

## Test plan
- **RED→GREEN** integration test (`resume_repo_rename_test.go`): start session →
  rename repo folder → resumed turn → commit still gets its trailer. Confirmed
  failing before the fix, passing after.
- Guard unit tests: main relocation reconciles; **linked-worktree session left
  untouched**; **resuming into a linked worktree left untouched**; live sibling
  untouched; same-path no-op.
- Full integration suite green; strategy pkg green; lint clean.

## Scope
Reconciliation only. Follow-ups from the issue (WARN on zero-match, `adopt`
without a live `--from`, `doctor` flagging stale paths) are deliberately left to
separate PRs.

- `prompt.txt`

- subagent transcripts and task descriptions (`task.json` records `transcript omitted by settings`)

- review prompts and investigate topics

## Design

- **Enforced at one seam:** `checkpoint.Open` wraps `Stores.Persistent` in `promptOmittingStore` (`checkpoint/prompt_omission.go`). Every persistent write path goes through it: condensation, finalize backfill, attach, import, and summary backfill. That covers both backends and mirrors. The wrapper preserves `AuthorReader`. ## Problem

`entire checkpoint explain --generate <hex-id>` under a git-refs primary generated the AI summary, then **discarded it**, and printed the misleading error `no checkpoint or commit found matching "<id>"` — for a checkpoint the same command had just displayed.

Root cause: `kindRoutingStore` kind-routes **reads** across both git backends (a hex ID under a git-refs primary reads refs, then falls back to the v1 branch), but **writes** always went to the configured primary. A pre-migration hex checkpoint that only exists on the v1 branch therefore resolved on read but failed every backfill with `ErrCheckpointNotFound` from the refs store.

## Fix

Backfill writes (`SessionSummary`, `SessionTranscript`, `CheckpointAttribution`) target an *existing* checkpoint, so they now follow the same store order reads use, falling through to the next store on `ErrCheckpointNotFound`:

- hex under git-refs primary → refs (via the mirror fan-out writer), then v1 branch
- ULID → always refs, regardless of primary
- a backfill landing on the primary still fans out to mirrors; one landing on a fallback store skips them (mirrors follow the primary)
- creates (`Session`) are unchanged — their ID is minted to match the primary's format

## Verification

- TDD: new `TestKindRoutingStore_*` tests written first (bug repro fails with `checkpoint not found` before the fix)
- Full unit suite green (8122 tests), `mise run fmt` + `mise run lint` clean

## Degradation semantics

On breach, capture proceeds with transcript-derived files. New-file detection is skipped for the turn: the `UntrackedScanSkipped` marker tells turn-end/subagent-end to drop `changes.New`, because without a pre-prompt baseline every untracked file in the worktree would be misattributed to the agent. This matters precisely in the cross-process shape — turn start breaches (marker written), turn end runs in a fresh process whose walk succeeds — and is covered by dedicated tests that fail if either guard is removed. Modified/deleted detection degrades to nil alongside the status error, as before. A breach inside the save itself (the C-git first-checkpoint read) skips that checkpoint with a Warn and still exits 0.

One deliberate widening beyond the budget feature: the pre-prompt/pre-task untracked scans now fail open on **any** error (repo-open failure, corrupted `.git`, …), not just budget breaches. Previously any status error there failed the TurnStart/SubagentStart hook and broke the agent's turn; that fail-hook behavior was the bug — the scan only feeds new-file detection, so the correct degrade is warn + marker + transcript-derived capture. The code comment at `untrackedFilesOrSkip` states this explicitly.

Degradation is visible outside `.entire/logs`: turn end persists `SessionState.CaptureDegradedAt` when any status scan feeding the turn breached (marker, `DetectFileChanges` sentinel, or a breach inside the save), and clears it on the next healthy turn. `entire status` prints a per-session warning ("capture degraded …: status scan over budget; new-file detection skipped") and `entire status --json` carries `capture_degraded` on the session brief, so a repo that breaches every turn no longer reports a healthy session while new-file detection is silently off.

- `TestStatusWithBudget_BreachAbandonsWalkPromptly` — breach surfaces the sentinel at the budget (not when the walk ends) and the latch stops a second walk from starting; pins the zombie regression.
- `TestStatusWithBudget_BreachWarnsWithRepoRoot` — the breach Warn carries the `repo_root` attribute (the incident was silent; this pins the observability).

## Why

The `checkpoint_version` stamp in each checkpoint's root `metadata.json` was a pure label: which storage backend serves a checkpoint is decided by the settings topology, and nothing ever dispatched on the stored value. The `EnsureCanReadVersion` read gates at resume/explain/rewind/export were forward-compat tripwires that could only fire for checkpoint formats that never shipped. Both are dead complexity — every reader had to thread a version through code that had exactly one possible answer.

Existing checkpoints' stored `checkpoint_version` values are handled by an external migration, so no backward-compat handling for the stored attribute is needed here.

## What changed

Removed the read gates first (they read the field), then the field itself: `WriteOptions.CheckpointVersion`, `CheckpointSummary.CheckpointVersion`, the stamping plumbing through the write chain, the read-side backfill (`normalizeCheckpointSummary`), and the now-unused `CheckpointVersionRefsV1` constant. Two follow-up cleanups: the hidden `entire checkpoint policy` help text now describes `checkpoint_version` as a write guard rather than a format selector, and the branch↔refs seam test regained a primary-read discriminator.

## Decisions made during development

- **The checkpoint policy subsystem is intentionally untouched.** Its `checkpoint_version` field remains a checkpoint-data write guard (`CanSatisfyPolicy`): a repo can still block writes from CLIs that don't support the configured version. It just no longer feeds a stamp into new summaries. `attach` switched from the deleted `checkpointVersionForNewCheckpoint` to the shared `ensureCheckpointPolicyAllowsCheckpointData` gate that explain and import already use.
- **`CheckpointVersionBranchV1` stays** — it anchors the policy defaults (`DefaultPolicy`, `Normalize`); only the refs-v1 constant became unused.
- **The seam test needed a new probe.** Dropping the version assert removed the only signal distinguishing a read served by the git-refs primary from one served by the git-branch mirror. The test now deletes the mirror's v1 branch and asserts the composed store still serves full reads — something only the primary can do.

## Reviewer notes

- Existing checkpoints and existing policy refs are left as-is; the stored-field cleanup ships as an external migration.
- Commits are ordered to be reviewable independently (gates → field → help text → seam test) and can be split into a stack if preferred.
